meta.title: Who really said "The past is but the beginning of a beginning"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — H.G. Wells wrote it, in his 1902 Royal Institution lecture “The Discovery of the Future.” The popular short form trims his hedged opening, “It is possible to believe that all…”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The past is but the beginning of a beginning'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely H.G. Wells — from his 1902 lecture “The Discovery of the Future.” The full line: “all the past is but the beginning of a beginning … the twilight of the dawn.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Wells’s lecture “The Discovery of the Future,” delivered at the Royal Institution on 24 January 1902 and published that year. The line is genuine, though the popular short form trims Wells’s hedged opening — his sentence begins “It is possible to believe that all the past is but the beginning of a beginning …”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Lecture at the Royal Institution, 24 Jan 1902; published 1902

source.excerpt: It is possible to believe that all the past is but the beginning of a beginning, and that all that is and has been is but the twilight of the dawn. It is possible to believe that all that the human mind has ever accomplished is but the dream before the awakening.
trail: The full sentence appears near the close of Wells’s “The Discovery of the Future” ↗: “all the past is but the beginning of a beginning … the twilight of the dawn.”
Wikiquote’s sourced H. G. Wells entry ↗ lists the line and credits “The Discovery of the Future.”
The lecture was delivered at the Royal Institution on 24 January 1902 and first published that year, per its publication history ↗ (also in Nature, 6 Feb 1902).
source.excerptNote: The closing passage of Wells’s lecture. The widely circulated quote lifts the first clause and drops the tentative frame — “It is possible to believe that all” — turning a speculation into a flat declaration.

source.rightsNote: “The Discovery of the Future” was first published in 1902 — well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — so the text, including this line, is in the public domain. (The Project Gutenberg edition is a 1913 U.S. reprint of the same public-domain work.)

author.name: H. G. Wells
author.heading: H. G. Wells
author.bio: Herbert George Wells (1866–1946) was an English writer whose science-romance novels — The Time Machine, The War of the Worlds, The Invisible Man — helped invent modern science fiction. He was also a prolific essayist and futurist; his 1902 Royal Institution discourse The Discovery of the Future argued that disciplined foresight could make the future as knowable as the past.

misattribution.heading: A real quote, but usually mis-worded
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Wells is correct — this is his line. What circulates is a trimmed and sometimes garbled version of it.

items.why: Quote sites drop Wells’s tentative opening. His sentence reads “It is possible to believe that all the past is but the beginning of a beginning” — a speculation, not the flat assertion the short form implies. See the full passage ↗.
Aggregators circulate garbled forms such as “The past is but the past of a beginning” and “The past is the beginning of the beginning,” e.g. on BrainyQuote ↗. Neither matches Wells’s actual wording.

misattribution.truthLine: Wells did write it — the accurate line is “all the past is but the beginning of a beginning, and all that is and has been is but the twilight of the dawn,” from “The Discovery of the Future” (1902) ↗.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Wells delivered The Discovery of the Future as a Friday-evening discourse at the Royal Institution on 24 January 1902. His argument: the future is not inherently unknowable — a disciplined, scientific habit of inductive foresight could make what is coming as legible as the recorded past.

The closing lines lift the argument into rhapsody. Set against the vast scale of cosmic and evolutionary time, Wells suggests all human history so far may be merely a prelude — “the twilight of the dawn,” “the dream before the awakening.” It is a hopeful, open-ended coda, which is why the fragment travels so well on its own.
context.pull: “All that is and has been is but the twilight of the dawn.”
